issues.legal_issue: Combining adjacent allotted plots and constructing a dwelling on each does not, without more, breach a lease condition prohibiting subdivision, more than one dwelling house on a plot, or commercial use.
material_facts: The lease-cum-sale agreement prohibited subdividing a plot, constructing more than one dwelling house on it, and using any part of the building as a shop, warehouse, or for specified commercial purposes.
The owners had sought permission to amalgamate their adjacent plots, but the request was rejected; the Court found no subdivision of either plot.
There was no finding that more than one building had been constructed on either plot or that any part of a building was being used commercially.
issues.conclusion: The alleged plot amalgamation did not violate the relevant lease condition, and the facts did not establish a breach through subdivision, multiple dwelling houses on a plot, or commercial use.
issues.legal_principle: The Court interpreted clause 4 of the lease-cum-sale agreement according to its stated prohibitions: subdivision, construction of more than one dwelling house on a plot, or specified commercial use. Amalgamation, even if it occurred, was not itself one of those prohibited acts.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_order and alleged_lease_breach_based_on_plot_combination and plots_not_subdivided and one_dwelling_per_plot and no_commercial_use_established

predicates.appeal_from_writ_order: A party appeals an order finding a breach of a site-related lease condition.
predicates.alleged_lease_breach_based_on_plot_combi: The alleged breach rests on combining or treating adjacent plots as a combined property.
predicates.plots_not_subdivided: The owners did not divide either plot into separate plots.
predicates.one_dwelling_per_plot: No more than one dwelling house was constructed on each plot.
predicates.no_commercial_use_established: The record does not establish that any part of the building was put to a prohibited commercial use.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns an alleged lease breach based on combining plots, and there was no subdivision, no more than one dwelling on each plot, and no established commercial use, the combination alone does not breach the lease condition.

issues.legal_issue: Departures from an approved building plan during unfinished construction do not by themselves establish an incurable violation when corrective changes can be made before permission to occupy is granted.
material_facts: The buildings remained under construction when the writ petition was filed and when the Court considered the dispute.
The municipal authority identified some deviations but stated that it would issue an occupancy certificate only after being satisfied that the construction complied with law.
The owners made changes, including partial demolition, while construction was incomplete and before an occupancy certificate had been granted.
issues.conclusion: It was premature to conclude that the buildings violated the sanctioned plans or the lease condition merely because deviations existed during construction; corrective measures could be taken before an occupancy or completion certificate was granted.
issues.legal_principle: Section 310 of the Karnataka Municipal Corporations Act, 1976, requires permission before a building may be occupied, subject to the provision’s terms. The Court explained that deviations do not necessarily make construction illegal if they can be corrected before an occupancy or completion certificate; an irremediable deviation may prevent that certificate from being granted. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_order and building_under_construction and corrective_changes_possible_before_occupancy and deviations_not_shown_irremediable

predicates.appeal_from_writ_order: A party appeals an order deciding the legality of ongoing building work.
predicates.building_under_construction: The building work was incomplete when the dispute was considered.
predicates.corrective_changes_possible_before_occup: The owner could still alter or correct the work before permission to occupy was granted.
predicates.deviations_not_shown_irremediable: The identified departures were not shown to be incapable of correction.

issues.definition: For an appeal concerning unfinished construction, correctable departures that are not shown to be irremediable do not, by themselves, establish illegal construction.

issues.legal_issue: A multi-storeyed dwelling is not prohibited by a lease condition limiting a plot to one dwelling house, provided the building is used for human habitation and complies with the applicable building requirements.
material_facts: The lease-cum-sale agreement defined a dwelling house as a building constructed wholly for human habitation and did not prohibit multi-storeyed construction.
The municipal authority stated that the modified plan was for residential use and that an occupancy certificate would be withheld unless the building complied with the plan and building regulations.
The buildings were incomplete, and commercial use had not been established.
issues.conclusion: The lease condition did not prohibit a multi-storeyed building used wholly for human habitation; no objection could be taken to such construction if it complied with the lease and applicable building regulations and bye-laws.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed clause 4 of the lease-cum-sale agreement as regulating the number and use of dwelling houses on a plot, not the number of storeys in a dwelling. Construction remained subject to the sanctioned plan and building regulations and bye-laws. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_order and multi_storeyed_building and building_used_for_human_habitation and building_complies_with_applicable_requirements

predicates.appeal_from_writ_order: A party appeals an order challenging the permissibility of a building under a site-related lease.
predicates.multi_storeyed_building: The building has more than one storey.
predicates.building_used_for_human_habitation: The building is used wholly as a dwelling for human habitation rather than for prohibited commercial purposes.
predicates.building_complies_with_applicable_requir: The building conforms to the applicable approved plan and building requirements.

issues.definition: A multi-storeyed building is permitted when it is used as a dwelling and complies with the applicable building requirements.

issues.legal_issue: A court should not routinely take over a statutory authority’s discretionary decision or direct a particular outcome without reasons showing that the authority cannot decide independently.
material_facts: The lease-cum-sale agreement gave the authority discretion to act in response to specified defaults or breaches, with notice and a hearing before a decision.
The High Court directed the authority to take action against the allottees without leaving the decision to the authority’s discretion.
The High Court gave no reason for concluding that the authority could not make an independent decision.
issues.conclusion: The direction requiring the authority to take action was beyond the High Court’s jurisdiction and was set aside; a court may displace the authority’s decision-making role only in exceptional circumstances supported by cogent reasons.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226, mandamus may compel performance of a public duty, but a court should not substitute its decision for a statutory authority’s independent discretion as a routine matter. If the authority has failed to exercise its own discretion, a court may quash its decision and require an independent decision. Only in exceptional circumstances, with reasons showing that the authority cannot decide independently or impartially, may the court itself take over the decision. The Court relied on Mansukhlal Vithaldas Chauhan v. State of Gujarat, (1997) 7 SCC 622; it also referred to Union of India v. S.B. Vohra, (2004) 2 SCC 150, and Saraswati Industrial Syndicate Ltd. v. Union of India, (1974) 2 SCC 630.

rule.if: court_reviewing_statutory_discretion and authority_has_discretion and court_directed_specific_outcome and no_cogent_reason_authority_cannot_decide_independently

predicates.court_reviewing_statutory_discretion: A court is reviewing the exercise or potential exercise of discretion by a statutory authority.
predicates.authority_has_discretion: The governing arrangement entrusts the authority with discretion to decide what action, if any, to take.
predicates.court_directed_specific_outcome: The court directed the authority to take a particular action rather than leaving the decision to it.
predicates.no_cogent_reason_authority_cannot_decide: The court gave no adequate reason why the authority could not decide independently or impartially.

issues.definition: When a court directs a specific outcome despite an authority’s discretion and gives no cogent reason the authority cannot decide independently, that direction taking over the authority’s role is unsustainable.

issues.legal_issue: Public interest litigation principles permit procedural flexibility in matters of grave public importance and good governance, while litigation essentially directed against an individual or organization should not be entertained, or should be entertained only rarely, when other remedies are available.
material_facts: The writ petition was directed principally against individual allottees and challenged construction on their plots.
The Court left open the question of the petitioner’s bona fides and did not decide whether the litigation qualified as public interest litigation.
The Court nevertheless addressed the general approach to procedural technicalities, good-governance issues, and litigation directed at an individual or organization.
issues.conclusion: The Court expressed no opinion on the petitioner’s bona fides or on the correctness of the High Court’s treatment of the petition as public interest litigation, but reaffirmed that courts should be more liberal in good-governance matters and should rarely entertain essentially individual-directed litigation when other remedies are available.
issues.legal_principle: Procedural technicalities are not automatically available as a defence in public interest litigation concerning grave public importance, though procedural law still applies. Courts should be somewhat more liberal in entertaining public interest litigation concerning good governance, but should not, or should only rarely, entertain matters essentially directed against one individual or organization when other remedies are available. The Court relied on Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P., 1989 Supp (1) SCC 504, and referred to R & M Trust v. Koramangala Residents Vigilance Group, (2005) 3 SCC 91.

predicates.litigation_is_public_interest_litigation: The proceeding is brought as a public interest litigation rather than solely as an inter partes dispute.
predicates.matter_of_grave_public_importance: The proceeding concerns an issue of grave public importance.
predicates.concerns_good_governance: The proceeding raises an issue pertaining to good governance.

issues.definition: In public interest litigation concerning grave public importance or good governance, procedural technicalities are not automatically a bar.
